common_name: Jefferson Elm (National Mall Disease-Tolerant American Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jefferson was propagated from a large surviving elm on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. and has shown outstanding Dutch elm disease tolerance in decades of USDA and National Park Service screening trials.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, leaving ample room for the tree's broad, arching, classic American elm canopy. Jefferson was propagated from a large, healthy elm that had survived for decades on the National Mall despite surrounding losses to Dutch elm disease, and subsequent inoculation trials by the National Park Service and USDA found it to carry some of the strongest documented disease tolerance of any American elm selection. It grows with the tall, vase-shaped silhouette that made the species a beloved street tree before the disease arrived, and it has performed well in compacted urban soils and polluted city conditions. Water deeply while the tree establishes, avoid wounding the trunk and roots, and prune while young to develop strong, well-spaced scaffold branches beneath the eventual high canopy.

common_name: Prairie Expedition Elm (Extreme-Cold-Hardy Disease-Tolerant American Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Prairie Expedition, released by North Dakota State University and named for the Lewis and Clark expedition, combines strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with exceptional cold hardiness well beyond that of most other resistant American elm cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the tree generous room to develop its wide, arching, classic elm canopy. Prairie Expedition was selected and released by North Dakota State University from a tree found growing on the grounds of a former fort, and was named for the Lewis and Clark expedition in recognition of its origins on the northern plains; it stands out among disease-tolerant American elm cultivars for surviving winters far colder than most others can handle, while still carrying good Dutch elm disease tolerance and glossy, dark green summer foliage. It restores the tall, graceful street-tree form long associated with American elm to regions where winter cold has ruled out many other resistant selections. Water deeply during establishment, provide good air circulation to reduce disease pressure, and prune while young to build a strong central framework.

common_name: Green Pillar Pin Oak (Narrow Columnar Pin Oak)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Pillar is a narrow, columnar selection of pin oak bred for tight urban sites where the species' normal wide-spreading, downswept form would be impractical.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, in tighter spaces than the species would otherwise tolerate. Green Pillar is a clonal selection of pin oak bred for a distinctly narrow, upright, columnar form, a striking departure from the wide-spreading, downswept branching that makes ordinary pin oaks unsuitable for many street medians, narrow boulevards, and tight residential lots. It keeps the species' fast growth, glossy deeply lobed foliage, and brilliant red fall color, along with its notable tolerance of wet, compacted clay soils. Because pin oak strictly requires acidic soil, avoid high-pH sites or amend with elemental sulfur to prevent iron chlorosis, and water deeply while the tree establishes its shallow, fibrous root system.

common_name: Sovereign Pin Oak (Upright-Branching Street Pin Oak)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Sovereign holds its lower branches more upright and horizontal than the species, reducing the low, drooping limbs that require frequent pruning over streets and sidewalks.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing room for a broad pyramidal canopy. Sovereign was selected for retaining the fast growth, symmetrical form, and glossy, deeply lobed foliage that make pin oak a popular urban shade tree, while holding its branches at a more ascending, horizontal angle instead of the species' characteristic downswept lower limbs, which greatly reduces the pruning needed to maintain clearance over streets, sidewalks, and parking areas. Fall color remains a strong brilliant red, and the tree keeps the species' excellent tolerance of wet, compacted clay soils and ease of transplanting. Because pin oak strictly requires acidic soil, avoid high-pH sites or amend with elemental sulfur to prevent iron chlorosis, and water deeply during establishment.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Wildfire, selected at the JC Raulston Arboretum, produces brilliant red new-growth flushes repeatedly through the growing season, not just in fall.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade. Wildfire, a selection introduced by the JC Raulston Arboretum at North Carolina State University, is prized for repeatedly flushing brilliant red new leaves on its shoot tips throughout the growing season, giving the canopy a shifting patchwork of red, orange, and green color from spring into summer rather than color limited to fall. It still delivers the species' outstanding, early-arriving scarlet fall display along with small dark fruit valued by songbirds. Black gum develops a deep taproot, so plant young container stock and avoid moving established trees; keep soil consistently moist and avoid high-pH sites that can cause chlorosis.

common_name: Red Rage Black Gum (Leaf-Spot-Resistant Glossy Tupelo)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Rage bears unusually glossy, dark green summer foliage with strong resistance to the leaf spot that often mars black gum, followed by reliable, early brilliant red fall color.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade. Red Rage was selected for exceptionally glossy, dark green leaves that resist the leaf spot fungus commonly seen on black gum by late summer, keeping the canopy cleaner and more attractive through the growing season, before turning an early and dependable brilliant scarlet in fall. It retains the species' small dark fruit that draws songbirds in early autumn and its adaptability to both moist bottomland and drier upland sites. Black gum develops a deep taproot, so plant young container stock and avoid disturbing established trees; keep soil consistently moist and avoid high-pH sites that can cause chlorosis.

common_name: Bosque Lacebark Elm (Single-Trunk Uniform Texas Shade Tree)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Bosque was selected for a single, straight trunk and a uniform, upright oval canopy, making it a popular alternative to live oak as a fast-growing shade and street tree across Texas and the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Bosque was selected from lacebark elm for a strong single trunk and a more uniform, upright-oval canopy than the multi-stemmed, spreading habit typical of seedling-grown lacebark elms, giving it a cleaner, more predictable form for street tree and shade tree rows. It shares the species' mottled, exfoliating gray-and-orange bark, fine-textured foliage, resistance to Dutch elm disease, and strong tolerance of heat, drought, and the alkaline clay soils common across Texas and the Gulf Coast. Structural pruning while young helps maintain the single leader and well-spaced scaffold branches that give this selection its tidy form; established trees need little supplemental water beyond normal rainfall.
